claim: Gpx4 mRNA levels are reduced in skeletal muscle biopsy samples from old humans compared to young humans.
source: (A, B) Glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4) mRNA levels in skeletal muscle biopsy samples from young and old humans (n=9 young [2 men and 7 women], n=18 for old [11 men and 7 women]) (A)
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1A with statistical comparison between young and old humans

claim: Gpx4 mRNA levels are reduced in gastrocnemius muscles from old mice compared to young mice.
source: (A, B) Glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4) mRNA levels in skeletal muscle biopsy samples from young and old humans (n=9 young [2 men and 7 women], n=18 for old [11 men and 7 women]) (A) or gastrocnemius muscles from young and old mice [n=8 for young, n=7 for old] (B).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1B with statistical comparison between young and old mice

claim: Aging promotes a robust increase in oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species in skeletal muscle.
source: Among these, age had the most robust effect on oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine (Figure 1C, red), a class of lipids that have been implicated as a potential lipid signal to induce ferroptosis (Kagan et al., 2017).
evidence: Oxidolipidomic analysis showing age-dependent changes in oxidized phospholipids, with citation to prior work on ferroptosis

claim: Six of the top ten oxidized lipid species with the most robust fold-increase with age were oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species.
source: Among the top ten oxidized lipid species whose abundance had the most robust fold-increase with age, six of them were oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of oxidized lipid species shown in Figure 1D

claim: Muscle 4-HNE levels are increased with age.
source: We confirmed increased muscle 4-HNE and MDA with age (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Western blot quantification and MDA assay data shown in Figure 1E-G

claim: Muscle MDA levels are increased with age.
source: We confirmed increased muscle 4-HNE and MDA with age (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Western blot quantification and MDA assay data shown in Figure 1E-G

claim: Hindlimb unloading induces muscle atrophy in mice.
source: As expected, HU-induced muscle atrophy and weakness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E) concomitant to reduction in body and lean mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Muscle mass and force measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E

claim: Hindlimb unloading induces muscle weakness in mice.
source: As expected, HU-induced muscle atrophy and weakness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E) concomitant to reduction in body and lean mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Force-frequency curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: Disuse robustly elevates muscle LOOH levels.
source: Disuse robustly elevated muscle LOOH levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G) without significant changes in mitochondrial ROS production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-J).
evidence: 4-HNE western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G

claim: Disuse does not significantly change mitochondrial ROS production.
source: Disuse robustly elevated muscle LOOH levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G) without significant changes in mitochondrial ROS production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-J).
evidence: Mitochondrial respiration and H2O2 production data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-J

claim: An increase in muscle LOOH precedes atrophy during hindlimb unloading.
source: An increase in muscle LOOH preceded atrophy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, F), consistent with the notion that LOOH may trigger mechanisms to promote loss of muscle mass.
evidence: Time course data showing LOOH increase at 1 day HU before significant atrophy at 7 days

claim: Lentivirus-mediated knockdown of GPx4 increases LOOH in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Lentivirus-mediated knockdown (KD) of GPx4 increased LOOH and markers of ferroptosis concomitant with a decrease in myotube diameter (Figure 2B–I).
evidence: 4-HNE and MDA measurements shown in Figure 2E-G

claim: GPx4 knockdown increases markers of ferroptosis in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Lentivirus-mediated knockdown (KD) of GPx4 increased LOOH and markers of ferroptosis concomitant with a decrease in myotube diameter (Figure 2B–I).
evidence: mRNA levels of Chac1 and Ptgs2 shown in Figure 2H

claim: GPx4 knockdown decreases myotube diameter in C2C12 cells.
source: Lentivirus-mediated knockdown (KD) of GPx4 increased LOOH and markers of ferroptosis concomitant with a decrease in myotube diameter (Figure 2B–I).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements shown in Figure 2B, C

claim: Erastin treatment increases LOOH in C2C12 myotubes.
source: We also recapitulated these findings with erastin (a system Xc- inhibitor that suppresses glutathione synthesis) (Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E)
evidence: 4-HNE and MDA measurements in erastin-treated cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Erastin is a system Xc- inhibitor that suppresses glutathione synthesis.
source: We also recapitulated these findings with erastin (a system Xc- inhibitor that suppresses glutathione synthesis) (Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E)
evidence: Description of erastin's mechanism of action

claim: RSL3 treatment increases LOOH in C2C12 myotubes.
source: and RSL3 (GPx4 inhibitor) (Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–I), commonly used acute pharmacological interventions to elevate intracellular LOOH.
evidence: Data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I

claim: RSL3 is a GPx4 inhibitor.
source: and RSL3 (GPx4 inhibitor) (Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–I), commonly used acute pharmacological interventions to elevate intracellular LOOH.
evidence: Description of RSL3's mechanism of action

claim: LOOH reduces myotube size in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: These data support the idea that LOOH reduces myotube size in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Inference from in vitro experiments showing direct effects of LOOH manipulation on myotube diameter

claim: GPx4 haploinsufficiency augments the loss in soleus mass induced by hindlimb unloading in young mice.
source: In young mice, GPx4 haploinsufficiency augmented the loss in soleus mass induced by HU (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Muscle mass data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Muscle masses between old Gpx4+/- and wildtype mice are not different.
source: However, muscle masses between old Gpx4+/- and wildtype mice were not different.
evidence: Comparison of muscle mass data in old mice shown in Figure 3A

claim: Disuse in old mice promotes an increase in LOOH that has reached a maximally effective threshold with age such that GPx4 deletion has no further effect.
source: We interpret these findings to mean that disuse in old mice promotes an increase in LOOH that has already reached a maximally effective threshold with age such that GPx4 deletion had no further effect.
evidence: Interpretation of the lack of difference in muscle mass between old Gpx4+/- and WT mice

claim: There are no differences in 4-HNE or MDA levels between old Gpx4+/- and wildtype mice.
source: In support of this, we saw no differences in 4-HNE or MDA levels between old Gpx4+/- and wildtype mice (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: 4-HNE and MDA measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G

claim: GPx4 haploinsufficiency does not alter force-generating capacity in old mice.
source: GPx4 haploinsufficiency did not alter force-generating capacity (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: Force-frequency curve data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J

claim: Soleus muscles from GPx4-MKO mice are more prone to developing disuse-induced atrophy.
source: Consistent with Gpx4+/- mice, soleus muscles from GPx4-MKO mice were also more prone to developing disuse-induced atrophy (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–F) concomitant to elevated LOOH (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, H), suggesting that loss of GPx4 in muscle augments atrophy in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Muscle mass and force data shown in Figure 3E, F

claim: Loss of GPx4 in muscle augments atrophy in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Consistent with Gpx4+/- mice, soleus muscles from GPx4-MKO mice were also more prone to developing disuse-induced atrophy (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–F) concomitant to elevated LOOH (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, H), suggesting that loss of GPx4 in muscle augments atrophy in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Inference from muscle-specific knockout experiments showing similar phenotype to global heterozygous knockout

claim: Reduced muscle mass in GPx4-MKO mice is consistent with reduced cross-sectional area of myofibers regardless of fiber-type compositions.
source: Histological analyses revealed that reduced muscle mass was consistent with reduced cross-sectional area (CSA) of myofibers regardless of fiber-type compositions (Figure 3H&I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2I, J).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 3H, I

claim: LOOH directly reduces muscle cell size in vivo.
source: These data implicate that LOOH directly reduces muscle cell size in vivo.
evidence: Inference from GPx4-MKO experiments showing reduced myofiber CSA

claim: GPx4 primarily neutralizes LOOH but also exhibits some activity toward other peroxides.
source: GPx4 primarily neutralizes LOOH but it also exhibits some activity toward other peroxides (Imai and Nakagawa, 2003).
evidence: Statement about GPx4 substrate specificity with citation

claim: LPCAT3 is an enzyme of Lands cycle that preferentially acylates lysophospholipids with PUFAs.
source: LPCAT3 is an enzyme of Lands cycle that preferentially acylates lysophospholipids with PUFAs, and thus an essential component of ferroptosis (Kagan et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of LPCAT3 function with citation

claim: LPCAT3 is an essential component of ferroptosis.
source: LPCAT3 is an enzyme of Lands cycle that preferentially acylates lysophospholipids with PUFAs, and thus an essential component of ferroptosis (Kagan et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about LPCAT3's role in ferroptosis with citation

claim: LPCAT3 knockdown rescues the increase in 4-HNE induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Indeed, LPCAT3 KD rescued the increase in 4-HNE induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements in double knockdown cells shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: LPCAT3 deletion completely restores the reduction in myotube diameter induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Remarkably, deletion of LPCAT3 KD completely restored the reduction in myotube diameter induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 4D&E).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements shown in Figure 4D, E

claim: LPCAT3 deletion prevents LOOH and cell death induced by erastin.
source: Similarly, LPCAT3 deletion also prevented LOOH and cell death induced by erastin (Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: 4-HNE and cell death measurements shown in Figure 4F-H

claim: Muscle atrophy induced by loss of GPx4 or erastin treatment is due to the accumulation of LOOH and not other peroxides.
source: These findings indicate that muscle atrophy induced by loss of GPx4 or erastin treatment is due to the accumulation of LOOH and not other peroxides.
evidence: Inference from LPCAT3 rescue experiments showing specificity for LOOH

claim: Erastin-induced reduction in myotube diameter is suppressed with bafilomycin A1.
source: Erastin-induced reduction in myotube diameter was suppressed with BafA1, but not with MG132 (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the lysosome mediates protein degradation by LOOH (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements with inhibitor treatments shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: Erastin-induced reduction in myotube diameter is not suppressed with MG132.
source: Erastin-induced reduction in myotube diameter was suppressed with BafA1, but not with MG132 (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the lysosome mediates protein degradation by LOOH (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements with inhibitor treatments shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: The lysosome mediates protein degradation by LOOH.
source: Erastin-induced reduction in myotube diameter was suppressed with BafA1, but not with MG132 (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the lysosome mediates protein degradation by LOOH (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from differential effects of lysosomal vs proteasomal inhibitors, with citation

claim: Autophagosome formation is mediated by lipidation of LC3 by ATG3.
source: Upstream of the lysosome, autophagosome formation is mediated by a lipidation of LC3 by ATG3 (Ichimura et al., 2000).
evidence: Statement about autophagy mechanism with citation

claim: GPx4 knockdown drastically reduces the protein content of p62, LC3-I, and LC3-II.
source: Indeed, GPx4 KD drastically reduced the protein content of p62, LC3-I, and LC3-II (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–H), potentially suggesting that LOOH either accelerates lysosomal degradation or reduces synthesis of these proteins.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C

claim: ATG3 knockdown completely rescues the reduction in myotube diameter induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Indeed, ATG3 KD completely rescued the reduction in myotube diameter induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements shown in Figure 5D, E

claim: Loss of ATG3 is protective from disuse-induced atrophy in soleus muscles.
source: Loss of ATG3 was protective from disuse-induced atrophy (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) in soleus and weakness (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) in soleus and EDL.
evidence: Muscle mass data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Loss of ATG3 is protective from disuse-induced weakness in soleus and EDL muscles.
source: Loss of ATG3 was protective from disuse-induced atrophy (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) in soleus and weakness (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) in soleus and EDL.
evidence: Force-frequency curve data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G

claim: The protective effect of muscle mass in soleus from ATG3 deletion is explained by greater myofiber cross-sectional area.
source: The protective effect of muscle mass in soleus was likely explained by greater myofiber CSA (Figure 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 6E, F

claim: Suppression of autophagy is sufficient to attenuate disuse-induced muscle atrophy and weakness.
source: Thus, suppression of autophagy is sufficient to attenuate disuse-induced muscle atrophy and weakness.
evidence: Inference from ATG3-MKO experiments

claim: Inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome axis by ATG3 deletion is sufficient to inhibit LOOH induced by GPx4 deletion.
source: Unexpectedly, quantification of 4-HNE revealed that inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome axis by ATG3 deletion or BafA1 was sufficient to inhibit LOOH induced by GPx4 deletion, erastin, or RSL3 (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements shown in Figure 7A-D

claim: Inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome axis by bafilomycin A1 is sufficient to inhibit LOOH induced by erastin.
source: Unexpectedly, quantification of 4-HNE revealed that inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome axis by ATG3 deletion or BafA1 was sufficient to inhibit LOOH induced by GPx4 deletion, erastin, or RSL3 (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements shown in Figure 7A-D

claim: The autophagy-lysosome axis is essential for LOOH amplification.
source: These findings suggest that the autophagy-lysosome axis is essential for LOOH amplification, in addition to its potential role in mediating protein degradation downstream.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing autophagy inhibition reduces LOOH

claim: 4-HNE is highly co-localized to LAMP2 in myotubes.
source: Indeed, immunofluorescence experiments revealed that 4-HNE is highly co-localized to LAMP2 (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), consistent with the notion that the lysosome is necessary for LOOH propagation.
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7E

claim: The lysosome is necessary for LOOH propagation.
source: Indeed, immunofluorescence experiments revealed that 4-HNE is highly co-localized to LAMP2 (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), consistent with the notion that the lysosome is necessary for LOOH propagation.
evidence: Inference from co-localization data and inhibitor experiments

claim: An increase in LOOH by hydrogen peroxide is completely inhibited by lysosomal inhibition.
source: To support this idea, an increase in LOOH by hydrogen peroxide or carmustine (agents that increase pan oxidative stress without acting on GPx4 directly) was completely inhibited by lysosomal inhibition (Figure 7F–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements with H2O2 and BafA1 shown in Figure 7F-H

claim: An increase in LOOH by carmustine is completely inhibited by lysosomal inhibition.
source: To support this idea, an increase in LOOH by hydrogen peroxide or carmustine (agents that increase pan oxidative stress without acting on GPx4 directly) was completely inhibited by lysosomal inhibition (Figure 7F–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements with BCNU and BafA1 shown in Figure 7F-H

claim: The propagation of LOOH may be mediated by the lysosome.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the propagation of LOOH may be mediated by the lysosome (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Inference from multiple experiments showing lysosomal involvement in LOOH accumulation

claim: Both young and old GPx4Tg mice are resistant to disuse-induced muscle atrophy.
source: Strikingly, both young and old GPx4Tg mice were resistant to disuse-induced muscle atrophy (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, G, greater effect in soleus than EDL).
evidence: Muscle mass data shown in Figure 8A

claim: GPx4 overexpression has a greater protective effect on muscle atrophy in soleus than EDL.
source: Strikingly, both young and old GPx4Tg mice were resistant to disuse-induced muscle atrophy (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, G, greater effect in soleus than EDL).
evidence: Comparison of muscle mass data between soleus and EDL

claim: GPx4 overexpression robustly protects young and old mice from muscle weakness induced by hindlimb unloading.
source: Perhaps even more impactful was the effect of GPx4 overexpression on skeletal muscle force-generating capacity such that, in both young and old, GPx4 overexpression robustly protected mice from muscle weakness induced by HU (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1H–J, soleus and EDL).
evidence: Force-frequency curve data shown in Figure 8B

claim: HU-induced increase in 4-HNE is completely suppressed in GPx4Tg mice.
source: Consistent with the notion that GPx4 overexpression acts on LOOH, HU-induced increase in 4-HNE was completely suppressed in GPx4Tg mice (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: 4-HNE western blot data shown in Figure 8C

claim: The protection from muscle atrophy in GPx4Tg mice is explained by greater myofiber cross-sectional area regardless of fiber type.
source: We also found that the protection from muscle atrophy was explained by greater myofiber CSA regardless of fiber type (Figure 8D&E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1L, M).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 8D, E

claim: Ferrostatin-1 inhibits the propagation of lipid peroxidation.
source: Ferrostatin-1 inhibits the propagation of lipid peroxidation and is widely used to study LOOH (Dixon et al., 2012; Codenotti et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of ferrostatin-1 mechanism with citations

claim: Incubation of cells with ferrostatin-1 is sufficient to suppress LOOH induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Indeed, incubation of cells with ferrostatin-1 was sufficient to suppress LOOH induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) concomitant with protection from myotube atrophy (Figure 8G&H and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: 4-HNE measurements shown in Figure 8F

claim: Ferrostatin-1 protects myotubes from atrophy induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Indeed, incubation of cells with ferrostatin-1 was sufficient to suppress LOOH induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) concomitant with protection from myotube atrophy (Figure 8G&H and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Myotube diameter measurements shown in Figure 8G, H

claim: L-carnosine is a dipeptide composed of beta-alanine and L-histidine that has the ability to scavenge reactive lipid aldehydes formed from LOOH.
source: Thus, we tested L-carnosine, a dipeptide composed of beta-alanine and L-histidine that has the ability to scavenge reactive lipid aldehydes formed from LOOH (Cripps et al., 2017; Everaert et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of L-carnosine structure and function with citations

claim: L-carnosine is sufficient to suppress 4-HNE and rescue cell death induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Similar to ferrostatin-1, L-carnosine was sufficient to suppress 4-HNE and rescue cell death induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–F) or erastin (Figure 8—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: 4-HNE and cell death measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D-F

claim: L-carnosine is sufficient to suppress 4-HNE and rescue cell death induced by erastin.
source: Similar to ferrostatin-1, L-carnosine was sufficient to suppress 4-HNE and rescue cell death induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–F) or erastin (Figure 8—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: 4-HNE and cell death measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2G-I

claim: L-carnosine treatment successfully suppresses 4-HNE induced by hindlimb unloading in mice.
source: L-carnosine treatment did not alter body mass, body composition, food intake, and water intake (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–D), and successfully suppressed 4-HNE induced by HU (Figure 8—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: 4-HNE western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3E, F

claim: Mice provided with L-carnosine are partly protected from disuse-induced atrophy in soleus muscles.
source: Remarkably, mice provided with L-carnosine were partly protected from disuse-induced atrophy in soleus muscles (Figure 8—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Muscle mass data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3G

claim: N-acetylcarnosine has a longer half-life than L-carnosine and may be a more effective reagent in humans.
source: In contrast, N-acetylcarnosine has a longer half-life and may be a more effective reagent in humans thus improving its translational potential.
evidence: Comparison of N-acetylcarnosine to L-carnosine properties

claim: N-acetylcarnosine prevents 4-HNE and cell death induced by GPx4 knockdown.
source: Similar to ferrostatin-1 and L-carnosine, N-acetylcarnosine also prevented 4-HNE and cell death induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C) or erastin (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: 4-HNE and cell death measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: N-acetylcarnosine prevents 4-HNE and cell death induced by erastin.
source: Similar to ferrostatin-1 and L-carnosine, N-acetylcarnosine also prevented 4-HNE and cell death induced by GPx4 KD (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C) or erastin (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: 4-HNE and cell death measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D-F

claim: N-acetylcarnosine successfully suppresses muscle 4-HNE in young and old mice.
source: Similar to L-carnosine treatment, N-acetylcarnosine did not alter body mass, body composition, food intake, or water intake (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–E), and successfully suppressed muscle 4-HNE (Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: 4-HNE western blot data shown in Figure 9B

claim: N-acetylcarnosine ameliorates atrophy in soleus muscles in both young and old mice.
source: Strikingly, similar to our findings in GPx4Tg mice, N-acetylcarnosine ameliorated atrophy in soleus (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2H) and weakness in both soleus and EDL (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2I–K) in both young and old mice.
evidence: Muscle mass data shown in Figure 9C

claim: N-acetylcarnosine ameliorates weakness in both soleus and EDL muscles in both young and old mice.
source: Strikingly, similar to our findings in GPx4Tg mice, N-acetylcarnosine ameliorated atrophy in soleus (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2H) and weakness in both soleus and EDL (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2I–K) in both young and old mice.
evidence: Force-frequency curve data shown in Figure 9D

claim: Protection from muscle atrophy by N-acetylcarnosine is explained by greater myofiber cross-sectional area regardless of fiber type.
source: Protection from muscle atrophy was similarly explained by greater myofiber CSA regardless of fiber type (Figure 9E, F and Figure 9—figure supplement 2L, M).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 9E, F

claim: Skeletal muscle LOOH is robustly upregulated with aging and disuse.
source: The current findings demonstrate a novel mechanism that indicate LOOH as a key downstream molecule by which oxidative stress promotes muscle atrophy and weakness. Skeletal muscle LOOH was robustly upregulated with aging and disuse, and genetic or pharmacological neutralization of LOOH and their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes was sufficient to rescue muscle atrophy and weakness.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings

claim: Genetic or pharmacological neutralization of LOOH and their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes is sufficient to rescue muscle atrophy and weakness.
source: The current findings demonstrate a novel mechanism that indicate LOOH as a key downstream molecule by which oxidative stress promotes muscle atrophy and weakness. Skeletal muscle LOOH was robustly upregulated with aging and disuse, and genetic or pharmacological neutralization of LOOH and their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes was sufficient to rescue muscle atrophy and weakness.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings from multiple experimental approaches

claim: N-acetylcarnosine treatment shows a potent effect in preserving muscle mass and strength with disuse in both young and old mice.
source: In particular, N-acetylcarnosine treatment shows a potent effect in preserving muscle mass and strength with disuse in both young and old mice, informing the potential trial to utilize this compound to ameliorate loss of muscle function in humans.
evidence: Summary of N-acetylcarnosine efficacy data

claim: Denervation and hindlimb unloading elicit different but overlapping responses in myofibers.
source: Denervation and HU elicits different but overlapping response in myofibers, and our studies demonstrate that their effects to drive skeletal muscle atrophy might converge on lipid peroxidation.
evidence: Comparison of different atrophy models

claim: The effects of denervation and hindlimb unloading to drive skeletal muscle atrophy might converge on lipid peroxidation.
source: Denervation and HU elicits different but overlapping response in myofibers, and our studies demonstrate that their effects to drive skeletal muscle atrophy might converge on lipid peroxidation.
evidence: Inference from comparison with Brown et al., 2022 study on denervation

claim: Liproxstatin-1 can suppress denervation-induced skeletal muscle atrophy.
source: During the preparation of this manuscript, Van Remmen and colleagues published a complementary study demonstrating that liproxstatin-1 can suppress denervation-induced skeletal muscle atrophy (Brown et al., 2022).
evidence: Citation to complementary study

claim: In vivo liproxstatin-1 treatment is highly effective in suppressing denervation-induced LOOH and reactive lipid aldehydes 4-HNE.
source: Nevertheless, in vivo liproxstatin-1 treatment was highly effective in suppressing denervation-induced LOOH as well as reactive lipid aldehydes 4-HNE, suggesting that targeting lipid peroxidation is likely an equally effective strategy to suppress LOOH production in skeletal muscle.
evidence: Discussion of findings from Brown et al., 2022

claim: Targeting lipid peroxidation is likely an equally effective strategy to suppress LOOH production in skeletal muscle.
source: Nevertheless, in vivo liproxstatin-1 treatment was highly effective in suppressing denervation-induced LOOH as well as reactive lipid aldehydes 4-HNE, suggesting that targeting lipid peroxidation is likely an equally effective strategy to suppress LOOH production in skeletal muscle.
evidence: Inference from comparison of different approaches to reduce LOOH

claim: The effect of lipid peroxidation to promote muscle atrophy is mediated by LOOH and their lipid reactive aldehydes.
source: Conversely, our data with GPx4 overexpression and N-acetylcarnosine treatment indicate that the effect of lipid peroxidation to promote muscle atrophy is mediated by LOOH and their lipid reactive aldehydes.
evidence: Inference from GPx4 overexpression and N-acetylcarnosine experiments

claim: Neither liproxstatin-1 nor ferrostatin-1 are currently FDA-approved.
source: Neither liproxstatin-1 nor ferrostatin-1 are currently FDA-approved, but it is worthwhile to consider these drugs along with N-acetylcarnosine as potential therapeutics to treat disuse-induced muscle atrophy.
evidence: Statement about regulatory status of compounds

claim: Inhibition of autophagy-lysosomal axis prevented myotube atrophy induced by erastin or GPx4 deletion.
source: Inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal axis prevented myotube atrophy induced by erastin or GPx4 deletion, and muscle atrophy and weakness induced by HU in vivo.
evidence: Summary of autophagy inhibition experiments

claim: Inhibition of autophagy-lysosomal axis prevented muscle atrophy and weakness induced by hindlimb unloading in vivo.
source: Inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal axis prevented myotube atrophy induced by erastin or GPx4 deletion, and muscle atrophy and weakness induced by HU in vivo.
evidence: Summary of ATG3-MKO experiments

claim: Previous studies have shown inhibition of autophagy accelerates muscle mass loss.
source: These findings are in contrast with previous studies that have shown inhibition of autophagy accelerates muscle mass (Carnio et al., 2014; Castets et al., 2013; Masiero et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to prior studies showing different effects of autophagy inhibition

claim: ATG3-MKO mice will eventually begin to undergo muscle atrophy similar to the muscle-specific ATG7 knockout model.
source: It is likely that ATG3-MKO mice will eventually begin to undergo muscle atrophy similar to the muscle-specific ATG7 knockout model (Masiero et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculation about long-term effects based on prior ATG7 knockout studies

claim: Inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal axis not only inhibits muscle atrophy but also the accumulation of LOOH.
source: Importantly, inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal axis not only inhibited muscle atrophy but also the accumulation of LOOH.
evidence: Summary of dual effects of autophagy inhibition

claim: The exact mechanism of the role of the lysosome in LOOH propagation is unclear.
source: The exact mechanism of the role of the lysosome in LOOH propagation is unclear, but our preliminary evidence shows LOOH accumulation occurring near the lysosome.
evidence: Acknowledgment of mechanistic uncertainty

claim: Skeletal muscle mass at 20 months of age is not significantly lower compared to 4 months of age.
source: While not statistically compared directly (these experiments were not performed side-by-side), skeletal muscle mass at 20 months of age was not significantly lower compared to those at 4 months of age.
evidence: Observation from muscle mass measurements across age groups

claim: Skeletal muscle force-generating capacity is lower in 20-month-old mice compared to 4-month-old mice, particularly in the extensor digitorum longus muscles.
source: Second, while muscle mass was not diminished at 20 months of age, skeletal muscle force-generating capacity was lower in 20-month-old mice compared to the 4-month-old mice, particularly in the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles.
evidence: Comparison of force measurements between age groups

claim: In GPx4Tg mice, age-associated decrease in muscle strength in non-HU mice appears to be rescued.
source: In GPx4Tg mice, age-associated decrease in muscle strength (in non-HU mice) appeared to be rescued, while short-term treatment with N-acetylcarnosine had no effect.
evidence: Comparison of force data in GPx4Tg mice across ages

claim: Short-term treatment with N-acetylcarnosine has no effect on age-associated decrease in muscle strength.
source: In GPx4Tg mice, age-associated decrease in muscle strength (in non-HU mice) appeared to be rescued, while short-term treatment with N-acetylcarnosine had no effect.
evidence: Comparison of force data in N-acetylcarnosine-treated mice

claim: In all experimental models in which accumulation of muscle LOOH was suppressed, force-generating capacity was more robustly rescued compared to skeletal muscle mass.
source: However, in all experimental models in which accumulation of muscle LOOH was suppressed (young and old GPx4Tg mice, young and old mice with N-acetylcarnosine, and young ATG3-MKO mice), force-generating capacity (i.e., specific force normalized to CSA) was more robustly rescued compared to skeletal muscle mass.
evidence: Comparison of muscle mass and force outcomes across multiple experimental models

claim: LOOH induces muscle weakness independent of muscle atrophy.
source: This suggests the role of LOOH to induce muscle weakness independent of muscle atrophy, and likely independent of muscle protein degradation.
evidence: Inference from differential effects on mass vs. force

claim: Reactive lipid aldehydes induced by aging or disuse may preferentially bind to enzymes of skeletal muscle contraction or excitation-contraction coupling to compromise their activities.
source: While out of the scope for the current study, it would be important to determine whether reactive lipid aldehydes induced by aging or disuse preferentially bind to enzymes of skeletal muscle contraction or excitation-contraction coupling to compromise their activities.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism for force loss

claim: Aging promotes muscle weakness prior to atrophy.
source: As described in the previous paragraph, aging promoted muscle weakness prior to atrophy.
evidence: Observation from age comparison data

claim: Muscle atrophy induced by cancer cachexia is preceded by muscle weakness.
source: Similarly, muscle atrophy induced by cancer cachexia is also preceded by muscle weakness (Delfinis et al., 2022).
evidence: Citation to study on cancer cachexia

claim: LOOH contributes to the loss of muscle mass and strength associated with age and disuse.
source: In conclusion, we provide evidence that LOOH contributes to the loss of muscle mass and strength associated with age and disuse.
evidence: Summary conclusion statement

claim: Neutralization of LOOH, particularly their reactive lipid aldehyde byproducts, attenuates muscle atrophy and weakness.
source: Neutralization of LOOH, particularly their reactive lipid aldehyde byproducts, attenuates muscle atrophy and weakness.
evidence: Summary of intervention studies

claim: The mechanisms by which LOOH contributes to muscle atrophy and weakness include protein degradation mediated by the autophagy-lysosomal axis.
source: The mechanisms by which LOOH contributes to these phenotypes are not entirely clear, but they include protein degradation mediated by the autophagy-lysosomal axis, as well as loss in the force-generating capacity that is likely mediated by carbonyl stress.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings

claim: The mechanisms by which LOOH contributes to muscle weakness include loss in force-generating capacity that is likely mediated by carbonyl stress.
source: The mechanisms by which LOOH contributes to these phenotypes are not entirely clear, but they include protein degradation mediated by the autophagy-lysosomal axis, as well as loss in the force-generating capacity that is likely mediated by carbonyl stress.
evidence: Inference from differential effects on mass vs. force and carbonyl scavenger experiments

claim: These findings inform a potential clinical trial to test the efficacy of N-acetylcarnosine treatment in ameliorating muscle atrophy in humans.
source: Last, but not least, these promising observations inform a potential clinical trial to test the efficacy of N-acetylcarnosine treatment in ameliorating muscle atrophy in humans.
evidence: Translational implication of the findings

claim: Reactive oxygen species accumulation is a cardinal feature of skeletal muscle atrophy.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation is a cardinal feature of skeletal muscle atrophy.
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing established knowledge

claim: It is unclear which downstream consequences of ROS are responsible for the loss of muscle mass and strength.
source: ROS refers to a collection of radical molecules whose cellular signals are vast, and it is unclear which downstream consequences of ROS are responsible for the loss of muscle mass and strength.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in abstract

claim: Lipid hydroperoxides are increased with age and disuse.
source: Here, we show that lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH) are increased with age and disuse, and the accumulation of LOOH by deletion of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4) is sufficient to augment muscle atrophy.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract

claim: The accumulation of LOOH by deletion of glutathione peroxidase 4 is sufficient to augment muscle atrophy.
source: Here, we show that lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH) are increased with age and disuse, and the accumulation of LOOH by deletion of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4) is sufficient to augment muscle atrophy.
evidence: Summary of GPx4 knockout experiments in abstract

claim: LOOH promotes atrophy in a lysosomal-dependent, proteasomal-independent manner.
source: LOOH promoted atrophy in a lysosomal-dependent, proteasomal-independent manner.
evidence: Summary of mechanism in abstract

claim: Genetic and pharmacological neutralization of LOOH or their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes robustly prevents muscle atrophy and weakness in young and old mice.
source: In young and old mice, genetic and pharmacological neutralization of LOOH or their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes robustly prevented muscle atrophy and weakness, indicating that LOOH-derived carbonyl stress mediates age- and disuse-induced muscle dysfunction.
evidence: Summary of intervention studies in abstract

claim: LOOH-derived carbonyl stress mediates age- and disuse-induced muscle dysfunction.
source: In young and old mice, genetic and pharmacological neutralization of LOOH or their secondary reactive lipid aldehydes robustly prevented muscle atrophy and weakness, indicating that LOOH-derived carbonyl stress mediates age- and disuse-induced muscle dysfunction.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments in abstract

claim: Loss of muscle mass and function with age is detrimental to health and quality of life.
source: Loss of muscle mass and function with age is detrimental to health and quality of life (Evans, 2010; Larsson et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of clinical significance with citations

claim: Sarcopenia is due to a combination of inactivity, injury, surgery, and biological consequences of aging.
source: Sarcopenia, muscle atrophy and weakness with aging, is due to a combination of inactivity, injury, surgery, and biological consequences of aging (Bonaldo and Sandri, 2013; Dolbow and Gorgey, 2016).
evidence: Definition and etiology of sarcopenia with citations

claim: A pharmacological therapy for muscle loss does not exist.
source: A pharmacological therapy for muscle loss does not exist, and current diet or exercise therapeutic approaches are often ineffective or unfeasible.
evidence: Statement of unmet clinical need

claim: Current diet or exercise therapeutic approaches for muscle loss are often ineffective or unfeasible.
source: A pharmacological therapy for muscle loss does not exist, and current diet or exercise therapeutic approaches are often ineffective or unfeasible.
evidence: Statement of limitations of current therapies

claim: Oxidative stress has been implicated in muscle atrophy by accelerating proteolysis.
source: Oxidative stress has been implicated in muscle atrophy by accelerating proteolysis (Powers et al., 2011; Scicchitano et al., 2018), but the exact mechanism by which reactive oxygen species (ROS) contributes to the decrease in muscle mass and strength is not well understood.
evidence: Statement of prior knowledge with citations

claim: The exact mechanism by which reactive oxygen species contributes to the decrease in muscle mass and strength is not well understood.
source: Oxidative stress has been implicated in muscle atrophy by accelerating proteolysis (Powers et al., 2011; Scicchitano et al., 2018), but the exact mechanism by which reactive oxygen species (ROS) contributes to the decrease in muscle mass and strength is not well understood.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap

claim: Lipid hydroperoxide is a class of ROS molecules that has been implicated in cell damage, particularly as a trigger to induce ferroptosis.
source: Lipid hydroperoxide (LOOH) is a class of ROS molecules that has been implicated in cell damage, particularly as a trigger to induce ferroptosis, a non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death (Wiernicki et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: Definition of LOOH with citations

claim: Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death.
source: Lipid hydroperoxide (LOOH) is a class of ROS molecules that has been implicated in cell damage, particularly as a trigger to induce ferroptosis, a non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death (Wiernicki et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: Definition of ferroptosis with citations

claim: Lipid peroxidation is initiated by prooxidants such as hydroxyl radicals attacking the carbon-carbon double bond in fatty acids, particularly the polyunsaturated fatty acids containing phospholipids.
source: Lipid peroxidation is initiated by prooxidants such as hydroxyl radicals attacking the carbon-carbon double bond in fatty acids, particularly the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) containing phospholipids (Bochkov et al., 2010).
evidence: Description of lipid peroxidation mechanism with citation

claim: LOOH is the primary product of lipid peroxidation that forms secondary reactive lipid aldehydes such as 4-hydroxynonenal and malondialdehyde.
source: LOOH is the primary product of lipid peroxidation that forms secondary reactive lipid aldehydes such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) and malondialdehyde (MDA), inducing carbonyl stress with high reactivity against biological molecules to promote cellular toxicity.
evidence: Description of LOOH products and their effects

claim: The intracellular level of LOOH is endogenously suppressed by glutathione peroxidase 4 that catalyzes the reaction by which LOOH is reduced to its nonreactive hydroxyl metabolite.
source: The intracellular level of LOOH is endogenously suppressed by glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4) that catalyzes the reaction by which LOOH is reduced to its nonreactive hydroxyl metabolite (Anderson et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of GPx4 function with citation

claim: The biological consequence of LOOH accumulation in skeletal muscle is not well understood.
source: Despite the evidence for the role of LOOH-mediated cell damage and cell death, the biological consequence of LOOH accumulation in skeletal muscle is not well understood (Bhattacharya et al., 2009; Pharaoh et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap with citations

claim: Germline deletion of GPx4 is embryonically lethal.
source: Germline deletion of GPx4 is embryonically lethal (Yant et al., 2003), but Gpx4+/- mice appear normal and do not have an observable muscle phenotype at baseline (Anderson et al., 2018; Katunga et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about GPx4 knockout phenotype with citation

claim: Gpx4+/- mice appear normal and do not have an observable muscle phenotype at baseline.
source: Germline deletion of GPx4 is embryonically lethal (Yant et al., 2003), but Gpx4+/- mice appear normal and do not have an observable muscle phenotype at baseline (Anderson et al., 2018; Katunga et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about Gpx4+/- phenotype with citations

claim: Oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine has been implicated as a potential lipid signal to induce ferroptosis.
source: Among these, age had the most robust effect on oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine (Figure 1C, red), a class of lipids that have been implicated as a potential lipid signal to induce ferroptosis (Kagan et al., 2017).
